column4: The ayah places human gestation and birth beside dead earth stirring and growing plants, directly joining the section’s womb-made body to its image of separate growth becoming living cover.
The believers are رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ and also a crop whose shoots strengthen one another, exactly fusing the section’s communal mercy with its connected-plant sense of تَوَاصَوْا.

Humanity spreads from one soul and its mate; the command to guard الْأَرْحَامَ appears with God as رَقِيبًا, bringing shared womb, kinship, descendants, and the section’s secondary رق ب sense into one ayah.
وَصَّيْنَا links counsel to parents while the mother carries and delivers in hardship, the Quranic meeting of the section’s birth oath, human كبد, and connected speech.
The counsel concerning parents recalls a mother carrying in weakness upon weakness and weaning the child, making parental bond and the bodily cost of lineage inseparable.

Spouses are created so that one may لِتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا, with affection and mercy between them; this states the section’s secondary sense of مسكين’s root as resting in a beloved and joins it to رحم.
A single soul finds repose in its mate, who then bears first a light and then a heavy pregnancy and prays for a sound child; dwelling, gestation, and offspring form one continuous scene.
Mothers nurse, the father provides, and neither parent may be harmed through the child; the ayah turns biological parenthood into a sustained network of care.
Creation from dust and a drop becomes paired life, pregnancy, and birth, all under divine knowledge; it gathers the section’s soil, lineage, womb, and visible or hidden gestation.
The human made from water is given both blood lineage and marriage affinity, directly naming the two relations by which birth extends into a connected human family.
God knows what every female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, grounding the section’s signs of approaching birth in hidden gestation and exact measure.
God forms people in the wombs as He wills; this is the direct Quranic setting for the section’s خ ل ق sense of a completed bodily form within the mother.
Creation after creation in three darknesses inside mothers’ wombs gives the hidden bodily sequence behind وَوَالِدٍ وَمَا وَلَدَ.
No female conceives or gives birth without God’s knowledge, setting the section’s outward signs of pregnancy against the divine knowledge that encompasses the whole event.
Mary’s mother speaks when she has delivered her child, and God knows best what she delivered; the ayah stages الولادة itself and the parent’s first relation to the newborn.
Mary conceives Jesus and withdraws with him to a distant place, presenting the hidden carrying that precedes the section’s act of birth.
Labor pains drive Mary to the palm trunk, making the hardship of delivery concrete and answering the section’s conjunction of birth with human كبد.
The human is placed as a drop in a secure resting place, locating created lineage within the protected bodily container described in the section as the child’s house.
Successive embryonic forms culminate in another creation, directly expanding the section’s خ ل ق sense from formed part to completed human life.
Creation moves from dust and a drop through a clot to emergence as a child, maturity, old age, and death; the full lineage-bearing life is shown as successive vulnerable stages.
God brings people from their mothers’ wombs knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, connecting birth to the section’s concern with what a human sees.
God grants daughters to some and sons to others, presenting offspring as a gift rather than the possession implied by human boasting.
God joins sons and daughters for some and makes others barren, marking both continuation and the threatened break in lineage developed through the section’s dictionary senses.
Zechariah asks not to be left alone without an heir, giving personal voice to the section’s image of solitary severance from continuing offspring.
God answers Zechariah, makes his wife fit, and describes the family hastening together in good works with hope and fear; restored lineage becomes a bound worshipping household.
The ayah rejects a false maternal claim by saying that mothers are only those who gave birth to them, using وَلَدْنَهُمْ to set the bodily boundary of parenthood.
لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ reverses both poles of the section’s human oath—begetting and being begotten—to mark the absolute boundary between created lineage and God.
Righteousness gives cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy, frees necks, keeps commitments, and remains patient; it assembles nearly the whole social ascent of 90:13–17.
Spending proceeds to parents, near kin, orphans, and the needy, showing how the biological relation of وَالِدَيْنِ widens into provision for those whose relations have failed.
Parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, near and distant neighbors, the companion at one’s side, and those under one’s hand form an expanding ring of nearness opposed to boastful pride.
The covenant places kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy together, the same movement from lineage to restorative care that the section hears across surah 90.
The ayah protects the orphan’s property, requires justice even toward ذَا قُرْبَىٰ, and closes with وَصَّاكُم, explicitly joining orphanhood, nearness, and binding counsel.
The same counsel sequence commands kindness to parents and forbids killing children because of poverty, protecting both ends of lineage where want could sever them.
The child asks God to show the parents mercy as they raised the child when small, returning رَحْمَة to the parent-child relation from which the section’s womb imagery begins.
This ayah requires gentle speech and honor when one or both parents reach old age; 17:24 then turns that long care into the child’s prayer for mercy.
وَصَّيْنَا الْإِنسَانَ بِوَالِدَيْهِ makes divine counsel itself carry the bond between the human and both parents, while also setting a boundary when they press for idolatry.
After the mother’s hardship in 31:14, the child must not obey parental idolatry but must accompany both parents honorably in this world; companionship preserves care without erasing moral limits.
Wealth and children do not bring people near to God; faith and good action do, directly correcting inherited or possessed nearness with the section’s final bond of belief and deed.
Belief and good works are sustained by mutual تَوَاصَوْا to truth and patience, the closest Quranic parallel to the section’s people becoming connected through shared counsel.
Abraham and Jacob وَصَّىٰ their sons with faith, making counsel a word carried through a family line rather than a merely private instruction.
الْوَصِيَّةُ is prescribed for parents and near relatives, concretely realizing the section’s dictionary image of a linked word that reaches across kinship.
The instruction about orphans says that setting their affairs right is best and that, if believers mix with them, they are their brothers; isolated children are deliberately rejoined to a household.
Abraham makes the word enduring فِي عَقِبِهِ, joining the section’s secondary sense of عقب as descendants who remain after a man to its image of speech passed onward.
Those praised connect what God commanded to be connected and fear their Lord, a direct thematic expression of the section’s movement from solitary rupture to maintained bonds.
Those condemned sever what God commanded to be joined, providing the exact reversal of the section’s تواصي as connection.
تُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ makes severed womb-relations the social consequence of corruption, the explicit opposite of mercy gathering people as if from one womb.
Breaking covenant and cutting what God ordered joined gives a second direct reversal of the section’s connected word, connected people, and continuous plant cover.
Believing men and women are protecting allies who enjoin right and receive God’s mercy; faith, reciprocal guidance, protection, and mercy become one community.
Believers are brothers, so fractured relations must be repaired and God feared so that mercy may be received; the ayah states the social kinship produced by faith.
God joins formerly hostile hearts so that people become brothers while all hold fast together, a direct nonlexical parallel to separate lives becoming one continuous cover.
God unites believers’ hearts in a bond that all the earth’s wealth could not purchase, clarifying why wealth cannot produce the nearness that faith produces.
A good word is a good tree with firm root and raised branches, joining the section’s connected speech to living growth in a single image.
The tree continually gives fruit by its Lord’s leave, completing 14:24’s account of how a rooted word persists and nourishes beyond its first speaker.
Creation from male and female becomes peoples and tribes so that humans may know one another, expanding birth into social familiarity rather than estrangement.
When Abraham’s son reaches the age of working beside him, father and son deliberate over the sacrifice and the son promises patience; grown companionship, filial counsel, and hardship meet here.
Luqman tells his son to establish prayer, enjoin right, forbid wrong, and be patient, making parental counsel the training ground for the patience later exchanged within a believing community.
Guardians test the orphans until maturity and release their property when they آنَسْتُمْ sound judgment; the root of familiarity or perception occurs precisely in care for the parentless child.
Believers may not enter others’ homes until تَسْتَأْنِسُوا and greet their people, turning non-estrangement into a concrete ethic of neighboring presence.
The Prophet tells his cave companion not to grieve because God is with them, and tranquility descends; companionship here visibly performs the section’s protection and removal of fear.
God feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear, bringing the feeding of want and the root sense of faith as fear’s removal into one compact pair.
Those who believe without clothing faith in wrongdoing receive الْأَمْنُ and guidance, explicitly deriving security from the same root as آمَنُوا.
أَصْحَابُ الْمَيْمَنَةِ repeats surah 90’s final designation, confirming that its newly bound people belong to an eschatological company.
After 74:38 makes every soul captive to what it earned, this ayah exempts أَصْحَابُ الْيَمِينِ, echoing the section’s move from an unfreed neck to a liberated company of the right.
The condemned confess that they did not feed the needy; beside 74:39, this identifies failure of the section’s feeding and mercy as what separates them from the company of the right.
أَتْرَابًا supplies the Quranic occurrence of the section’s secondary ترب sense, people of matching age who belong together rather than a poor person cast into dust.
The companions kept near in the garden are أَتْرَابٌ, another direct use of the section’s soil-root in its peer and age-mate sense.
أَتْرَابًا again names equal-aged companions, completing the Quran’s repeated evidence for the secondary ترب sense developed by the section.
A wall protects treasure for two orphan boys until maturity because their father was righteous; a dead parent’s care is carried forward by God and a compassionate stranger.
God finds the Prophet an orphan and gives shelter, the clearest reversal within life of the section’s orphan as one left alone by parental loss.
The command not to oppress the orphan turns recognition of parental rupture into the protective conduct demanded by the section.
Food is given despite love for it to the needy, orphan, and captive, closely matching the ascent through feeding and release toward a merciful company.
Expiation for a broken oath includes feeding the needy or freeing a neck, bringing oath, provision, and تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ together as surah 90 does.
Accidental killing is answered by freeing a believing neck and compensation delivered to the victim’s family, joining a life cut off, surviving kin, and emancipation as repair.
A man retracting words that confused wife with mother must free a neck before the couple touch, placing emancipation beside the guarded boundary between marriage and motherhood.
Believing descendants are joined to believing parents without diminishing anyone’s deeds, giving the section’s threatened lineage an image of final reunion through faith.
The righteous enter lasting gardens together with righteous parents, spouses, and descendants, so kinship and moral formation culminate in a gathered household.
The angels ask that believers be admitted with the righteous among their parents, spouses, and descendants, making mercy the force that reunites generations.

Calling adopted children by their fathers preserves actual lineage, while those whose fathers are unknown become brothers in faith and close associates; biological and chosen bonds are carefully joined.
Pregnant women must be housed and maintained until delivery, and nursing is arranged by mutual consultation, turning approaching birth into continued social provision.
Following the mother’s hardship in 46:15, the grown child asks that offspring be made righteous and is accepted among the garden’s companions; care passes forward through generations.
Blood relatives are declared nearer to one another while later believers still belong to the faithful community, defining the relationship between womb-nearness and chosen fellowship.
The Prophet is nearer to believers and his wives are their mothers, yet blood relatives remain nearer by divine ordinance; communal and genealogical kinship are held together without confusion.
The relative receives a due alongside the needy and traveler, translating nearness into provision for both kin and socially exposed people.
Giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due is named as the course that seeks God’s face, so proximity becomes an enacted bond rather than mere descent.
Justice and excellence culminate in giving to near kin, a concise command that turns the section’s root of nearness into social mercy.
God has grown humans from the earth like a growth, giving direct Quranic form to the section’s movement from a lone earthen figure into joined vegetation.
God knows humans both when they arise from earth and when they are embryos in their mothers’ wombs, joining the section’s soil and gestational images under one knowledge.
Creation from dust is followed by humans spreading abroad, so the solitary material origin becomes a dispersed and multiplying human population.
The ayah denies that a wife called “mother” becomes a mother or that an adopted son becomes a biological son, guarding the meanings of womb, birth, and lineage on which the section depends.
أَتَوَاصَوْا بِهِ asks whether rejecting generations passed their falsehood to one another, turning the section’s mutually sustaining counsel into a transmitted bond of rebellion.
Failing to honor the orphan is presented as a moral exposure, the opposite response to the severed child whom surah 90 places on the ascent.
The failure to urge one another to feed the needy reverses both the section’s feeding and its reciprocal counsel.
The denier violently repels the orphan, intensifying the section’s image of a child already severed from a father into deliberate social exclusion.
Not urging the feeding of the needy is the negative counterpart to feeding in surah 90 and mutually binding people through mercy.
At the trumpet there are no lineage ties between people and no mutual questioning, an eschatological boundary on the earthly continuity named by parent, child, and descendants.
On that Day a person flees from his brother, beginning the dissolution of the family network that the section works to bind.
A person also flees mother and father, reversing the originating parent-child bond of وَالِدٍ وَمَا وَلَدَ.
Flight from spouse and children completes the scene of kinship unable by itself to hold people together at judgment.
Neither relatives nor children benefit people on the Day of Resurrection, setting a limit on descent as saving nearness and reinforcing 34:37’s correction.
Killing children for fear of poverty is forbidden because God provides for parent and child, the starkest deliberate severing of lineage at the point where need should summon care.
The buried infant girl is brought forward and questioned, giving a face to offspring whose life and lineage were violently cut off.
The question “for what sin was she killed?” exposes the injustice in 81:8 and makes the destruction of a child answerable before God.
The father’s face darkens at news of a daughter, showing parenthood received as shame rather than the entrusted bond developed by the section.
Hiding from people and considering burying the daughter turns estrangement into lethal severance, completing 16:58’s reversal of parental mercy.

After 46:15–16 trace a mother’s hardship and a grateful child’s prayer for descendants, this child says contemptuously to both parents and rejects their warning, staging filial connection broken from within.
Worldly life is vegetation that flourishes with rain and then becomes scattered debris, a temporal reversal of the section’s continuous green cover.
Boasting and rivalry in wealth and children are compared to vegetation that delights and then withers, setting transient offspring-pride against the enduring bond of faith and mercy.
The foremost are الْمُقَرَّبُونَ, extending the section’s nearness root from blood relation to the nearness granted by faithful action.
The human is declared in loss; 103:3 then identifies faith, good action, and reciprocal counsel as the relations that keep a person from remaining isolated in that loss.
Luqman’s tender address to his son begins a sustained act of counsel, showing how a linked word first passes within a parent-child relation.
Luqman tells his son that even a mustard-seed deed hidden in rock will be brought forth by God, answering the section’s question whether anyone sees before 31:17 commands patience.
Zechariah fears what will follow him while his wife is barren and asks for an heir, combining succession with the possibility that lineage will stop.
The requested child will inherit from Zechariah and Jacob’s house, specifying the continuing عقب sought in 19:5.
The promise of Yahya answers the threatened break in 19:5–6 with a named child and renewed descent.
Sarah receives news of Isaac and, after Isaac, Jacob, making childbirth also the promise of a grandchild who remains after the first generation.
Abraham’s wife strikes her face and calls herself old and barren, voicing the bodily impossibility against which promised birth renews lineage.
Noah’s descendants are made the survivors, a large-scale instance of عقب as children remaining after catastrophe.
Wealth and children are adornment, while lasting good deeds are better; after 18:45’s scattered vegetation, the ayah distinguishes inherited display from what truly remains.
God promises believing doers of good that fear will be exchanged for security, unfolding the section’s root definition of faith as fear’s departure at communal scale.
Tranquility descends into believers’ hearts and increases faith, closely matching the section’s definition of security as the soul becoming calm.
Those already settled make room in their hearts for migrants and prefer them despite their own need, a concrete social passage from estrangement and poverty to protected companionship.
Believers must guard themselves and their families from the Fire, turning family attachment into responsibility for the lives that follow them.
Ishmael commands his household to prayer and almsgiving, another instance of guidance carried through the family relation.
The Prophet is told to command his family to prayer and persist in it, pairing household guidance with the patience that the section’s believers exchange.
